script: [serious] In the late 1910s, in a factory in Orange, New Jersey, young women were told to put radioactive paint in their mouths. Hundreds of times a day. And they were told it was safe. Within a few years, their teeth were falling out and their jaws were crumbling. The radium dust made them glow in the dark. Their bosses said it was something else. Doctors hired by the company told them so too. And then a small group of dying women decided to sue one of the most powerful industries in America. By the end of this file, you'll see the report the company hid, the bones that gave the secret away, and the courtroom where the women were too sick to raise their hands. Radium was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898. It glowed. It gave off energy, apparently forever. And in the early 1900s, the public went wild for it. It was sold in tonics, in face creams, in toothpaste, and in water you could drink for your health. Doctors used it to treat cancer, and many people believed that a little radium was good for you. One of its most popular uses was luminous paint. Mixed with zinc sulfide, a tiny amount of radium made a paint that glowed in the dark. The U.S. Radium Corporation sold it under the name Undark. And when America entered the First World War, the military needed thousands of watches and instrument dials that soldiers could read at night. Even the man who invented Undark, Sabin von Sochocky, was not safe. He died of radium poisoning in 1928. But in those early years, the company hired young women, many of them teenagers, to paint the numbers by hand. The work paid well, by the piece, and it was considered a glamorous job. The brushes were made of fine camel hair, and the numbers were tiny. To keep a sharp point, the women were taught a technique. Lip, dip, paint. Shape the brush between your lips, dip it in the radium paint, paint a number, and repeat. Over and over, all day long. Some of the women painted around two hundred and fifty dials a day. They swallowed small amounts of radium every day. They were told it was harmless. Some of them painted their nails and teeth with it for fun, and went home glowing. Dust from the paint covered their hair and clothes. Meanwhile, in the same company, the chemists who handled radium used lead screens, masks and tongs. Radium, it turned out, acts a lot like calcium in the body. Once swallowed, it settles into the bones. And there, it keeps on giving off radiation, day after day, for years. Around 1922, the first painters started getting sick. Teeth fell out. Sores wouldn't heal. Jawbones began to crumble and break apart. A former painter named Mollie Maggia died that year. Her death was blamed on syphilis. A dentist in New York, who saw several of the women, began to suspect their work, and called it radium jaw. The company commissioned a study by experts from Harvard. In 1924, they reported that the paint was very likely the cause. According to the historians who later studied the case, the company's president did not share that conclusion. Instead, a report was given to state officials that said the workers were in good health. Then, in 1925, the medical examiner of Newark, Harrison Martland, developed tests that could detect radioactivity in a living person's breath. He found it in the painters, and in the bones of women who had already died. It was the first time anyone had shown that radium could build up inside the human body. And he concluded that the radium inside them was what was destroying their bodies. In 1927, Mollie Maggia's body was exhumed. Her bones were radioactive. It had never been syphilis. By then, a former painter named Grace Fryer had been looking for a lawyer for two years. Most were afraid to take on the radium industry. Finally, in 1927, a young lawyer named Raymond Berry agreed. The company's first defense was the clock. Under New Jersey law, workers had only a limited time to sue after an injury, and the company argued the women had waited too long. But radium poisoning took years to appear. The women couldn't have sued for an injury no one would admit they had. Four other women joined her: Edna Hussman, Katherine Schaub, and two sisters of Mollie Maggia, Quinta McDonald and Albina Larice. The newspapers called them the Radium Girls, and the story spread around the world. Even Marie Curie was asked about them. She was reported to say that once radium got into the body, there was no known way to remove it. The women understood what that meant. They were not suing to be cured. They were suing so that someone would admit what had happened. The company's lawyers tried to delay, knowing the women might not live long enough to win. At one hearing, some of the women were too sick to raise their arms to take the oath. In 1928, the company settled. Ten thousand dollars each, a yearly payment of six hundred dollars, and their medical and legal costs. None of the five lived to old age. Most were dead within a decade. But it wasn't over. In Ottawa, Illinois, another company, Radium Dial, had used the same methods. In 1938, a dying former painter, Catherine Donohue, won her case, just months before she died. Part of the hearing was held at her home, because she was too ill to travel. The company kept appealing until 1939, and lost. The Radium Girls changed American law. Their cases helped establish the right of workers to sue their employers for diseases caused by their jobs. And when scientists built the atomic bomb in the 1940s, the studies of the dial painters helped shape the first safety limits for radiation inside the body. For decades afterwards, researchers studied the dial painters who were still alive, measuring the radium in their bodies to learn how much it took to cause harm. Many of those women volunteered, knowing it would not help them, but might help someone else. In a way, they protected the workers who came after them. So here is what the file tells us. The danger wasn't hidden from everyone. The chemists protected themselves. The company had a report that named the cause. What the painters didn't have was the truth, until they fought for it. If you had been told your job was safe, how long would it take you to believe otherwise? Tell me in the comments. This is Dossier Decoded.
